pl-l2d24c12-d1e105.summary: States that when the woman eats without the man, the sin is sometimes mortal, sometimes venial.
claims: Lower reason's consent may be mortal or venial.

pl-l2d24c12-d1e108.summary: Explains: the woman eats without the man when sin is held in delight of thought without being resolved on, or when the man sets a limit. If it is not held long but repelled by the man's authority as soon as it touches the woman, it is venial; if held long in delight, even without will to accomplish, it is mortal, and both man and woman, the whole person, are damned, since the man did not restrain the woman and so may be said to have consented.
claims: Prolonged delight in sinful thought is mortal.
Immediate rejection makes it venial.

pl-l2d24c12-d1e113.summary: Summarizes: when sin is conceived so that one plans or does it (some sins even once, others if frequent), or holds it long in delight of thought, it is mortal; when it is only in sensual motion it is very light, since reason does not delight. Some things damn even if done or planned once, others only if often, as idle words.
claims: Sins mortal once vs only if habitual.
Sensual motion alone is very light.

pl-l2d24c12-d1e117.summary: Cites De Trinitate XII: as in the first marriage the serpent persuaded and the woman gave to her husband, so in the secret marriage in each person, when animal sense offers an allurement to the reason of knowledge, the serpent speaks to the woman; consenting is eating; if the consent is content with delight of thought while the members are restrained, the woman alone has eaten.
claims: Consent in delight of thought alone is the woman eating.

pl-l2d24c12-d1e122.summary: Continues Augustine: if consent decides to carry out the sin if possible, the woman has given to her husband, since the mind's power over the members yields. Delighting in illicit thoughts, though not deciding to act, is sin, though much less, and requires forgiveness ('forgive us our debts'). Unlike the first couple, each bearing their own person, in one person the whole man is damned unless such sins of thought are remitted through the Mediator's grace.
claims: Delight in illicit thoughts is sin.
The whole person is condemned unless forgiven through Christ.

pl-l2d24c12-d1e125.summary: Cites Augustine against the Manichees: the devil does not appear visibly but suggests by thought, as he entered Judas's heart; man repels him if he guards paradise, but he deceives through the woman, since reason cannot be led to consent unless delight is stirred in the part that should obey reason as a husband. First comes suggestion by thought or senses; if desire is not moved, the serpent is excluded; if moved, the woman is persuaded; if reason restrains desire, we are crowned after struggle; if it consents and decides to act, man is expelled from paradise, sin being imputed even without the deed.
claims: Suggestion, delight, and consent are the stages of sin.
Consent of reason is sin even without the deed.
Resisting stirred desire earns a crown.

pl-l2d24c12-d1e130.summary: Explains that this discussion of the soul's parts shows by which part free choice exists, namely reason, by which every mortal sin is committed, but not every venial, such as that which exists only in sensual motion.
claims: Free choice resides in reason.
Every mortal sin involves reason; some venial sins do not.

pl-l2d24c12.summary: Holds that when the woman eats without the man, the sin is sometimes mortal, sometimes venial: venial if the sin is repelled by the man's authority as soon as it touches the woman; mortal if held long in delight of thought, even without will to act, since then the man did not restrain the woman and may be said to have consented, and the whole person is damned. In sum: mortal when sin is conceived to be done, or done (some things even once, others only if often), or long held in delight of thought; very light when only in sensual motion. Augustine, De Trinitate XII: the secret marriage in each person; delight in illicit thoughts, though less than resolving to act, is sin and needs forgiveness ('forgive us our debts'), and the whole person is damned unless forgiven through the Mediator. Contra Manichaeos: the devil suggests through thought; we fall through the woman when delight is stirred in the part that should obey reason; if reason restrains, we are crowned; if it consents, we are expelled from paradise. Free choice is in reason, by which all mortal sin is committed, but not all venial.
claims: When the woman eats alone, the sin may be venial or mortal.
It is venial if immediately repelled by higher reason.
It is mortal if long held in delight of thought, even without will to act.
The whole person, not the lower reason alone, is condemned.
Some sins are mortal even once; others only if repeated.
Delight in illicit thoughts is sin requiring forgiveness.
Free choice resides in reason, by which every mortal sin is committed.
